entry: Jewish holiday commemorating the Maccabean Revolt against the [[Seleucid Empire]] and the rededication of the Temple in [[Jerusalem]]. Beginning on the 25th of Kislev in the [[Hebrew calendar]], it lasts eight nights, with one more light kindled each night on a nine-branched menorah, using the *shamash* helper candle. It is the only Jewish holiday that starts in one month and ends in another. Relatively minor in religious terms, it has major cultural significance in the [[Western world]], especially among secular Jews, as it often falls near [[Christmas]].

Deity in [[Hinduism]] and devoted companion of the god [[Rama]], also known as Maruti and Bajrangabali. Hanuman is a *vanara*, a monkey-like being, and a central figure of the [[Ramayana]], celebrated for unwavering devotion to Rama. In most Vaishnava traditions he is the son of the wind god Vayu, while in Shaiva tradition he is an incarnation of [[Shiva]]. Devotional worship centered on him emerged roughly a millennium after the Ramayana was composed, and he is revered as an exemplar of self-control, faith and commitment to a cause. Traditionally he is celebrated as a lifelong celibate.

American television sitcom (1974–1984). Created by Garry Marshall, it ran for 255 half-hour episodes over 11 seasons on ABC, set in [[Milwaukee]], [[Wisconsin]], in the 1950s and 1960s. Its teenage lead, Richie Cunningham, was played by [[Ron Howard]]. After ratings fell in the second season, the show was retooled to spotlight Fonzie, a biker and high school dropout played by Henry Winkler, and it became the number-one program on television in 1976–1977. It spawned the spin-offs *Laverne & Shirley* and *Mork & Mindy*.

Clade of mostly unicellular marine [[Algae|algae]], also called Haptophyta or Prymnesiophyta. Haptophytes are distinguished by a haptonema, a flagellum-like organelle used for attachment and prey capture, alongside two smooth [[Flagellum|flagella]]. Their [[Chloroplast|chloroplasts]] contain chlorophylls a, c1 and c2 and fucoxanthin, which is likely the main cause of their brownish-yellow color. The best-known members are coccolithophores, which make up 673 of the 762 described haptophyte species and are covered in calcareous plates called coccoliths. Their remains form [[Chalk]] deposits. Some planktonic species, such as *Prymnesium*, form toxic blooms, while *Pavlova lutheri* and *Isochrysis* sp. are widely used in [[Aquaculture]] to feed [[Oyster|oyster]] and [[Shrimp|shrimp]] larvae.

Arabic term meaning sinful or prohibited, and one of the five rulings in Islamic jurisprudence. In Islam, *ḥarām* denotes any act forbidden by God, prohibited in the [[Quran]] and [[Hadith|hadith]], and the sunnah category of haram is the highest status of prohibition. Something haram remains prohibited whatever the intention. The term also means something set aside or sacred, to which access is not allowed to those not in a state of purity. Haram acts are a [[Sin|sin]] when committed by a Muslim; examples include [[Murder|murder]], [[Theft|theft]] and [[Gambling|gambling]]. Ill-gotten wealth, including money earned through [[Interest (economics)|interest]], is also haram. Legal schools differ on what is haram, depending on their interpretation of the Quran and hadith.

Capital and largest city of [[Zimbabwe]]. Harare lies in the northeast of the country, in the Mashonaland region, on a plateau at 1,483 m (4,865 ft). The city proper had a population of 1,849,600 at the 2022 census. Founded in 1890 by the Pioneer Column, a military force of the British South Africa Company organized by [[Cecil Rhodes]], it was named Fort Salisbury. It became the capital of the self-governing colony of Southern Rhodesia in 1923 and was renamed Harare in 1982, two years after Zimbabwe's independence from the [[United Kingdom]]. Today it is the country's financial, economic, industrial and communications hub. The [[World Health Organization]] had its African headquarters there until 2006, and the city hosted the 2003 [[Cricket World Cup]].

Capital and largest city of Heilongjiang province, northeastern China. By urban population Harbin is the second largest city in Northeast China, after [[Shenyang]], and it has the region's largest metropolitan population. It was the eighth most populous Chinese city in the 2020 census. Founded in 1898 with the Russian-built Chinese Eastern Railway, the city was settled largely by immigrants from the [[Russian Empire]]. In the 1920s it was considered China's fashion capital, as designs from [[Paris]] and [[Moscow]] reached it before [[Shanghai]]. From 1932 until 1945 it was the largest city in the Japanese puppet state of [[Manchukuo]]. Known as the Ice City for its winter tourism and ice sculpture festival, Harbin hosted the 1996 Winter Asian Games.

Sheltered part of a [[Body of water|body of water]] for mooring boats, ships and [[Barge|barges]]. The term is often used interchangeably with [[Port|port]], although a port refers specifically to facilities for loading and unloading ships. Harbors may be natural, surrounded on several sides by land, or artificial, built with breakwaters, sea walls or jetties, or created by dredging. The oldest known artificial harbor is an Ancient Egyptian site at Wadi al-Jarf, on the Red Sea coast, at least 4500 years old. The largest is Jebel Ali in [[Dubai]]. Natural examples include [[Victoria Harbour]] in [[Hong Kong]], Sydney Harbour and Halifax Harbour. Long Beach Harbor, [[California]], was salt marsh until it was first dredged in the early 20th century. The world's southernmost harbor, at Winter Quarters Bay in [[Antarctica]], is sometimes ice-free.

Electro-mechanical data storage device, also called a hard disk, hard drive or fixed disk. Rigid platters coated with magnetic material spin rapidly, and heads on a moving actuator arm read and write data in random order. HDDs are non-volatile, retaining data when powered off. [[IBM]] introduced the first disk drive, the 350, in 1956 as part of the 305 RAMAC system, and disks were the dominant secondary storage for general-purpose computers from the early 1960s. HDDs remain dominant for bulk storage on servers, although [[Solid-state drive|solid-state drives]] (SSDs) are faster and have replaced them where speed, power consumption and durability matter. Capacity is stated in decimal units, so a 1-terabyte drive holds 1,000 gigabytes, while operating systems often report capacity in powers of 1024 and show a smaller number.

[[Pornography]] featuring detailed depictions of sexual organs or sexual acts, in contrast to less-explicit [[Softcore pornography|softcore]] material. It usually takes the form of magazines, photographs, films and cartoons, and since the mid-1990s it has been widely available on the internet, much of it free of charge. In the 1950s and 1960s American jurists distinguished it from "borderline" pornography, and in Jacobellis v. Ohio (1964) the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that only hardcore material could be prohibited under obscenity laws. Studies have linked frequent consumption to lower relationship satisfaction, and whether it causes such effects remains debated.

[[Mammal|Mammals]] of the genus *Lepus*, in the order [[Lagomorpha]]. Hares are swift [[Herbivore|herbivores]] that live solitarily or in pairs and rest in shallow depressions called forms. They can run up to 80 km/h (50 mph) over short distances, with long, powerful hind legs and large ears that dissipate body heat. Native to Africa, Eurasia and North America, the genus includes the largest lagomorphs. Compared with [[Rabbit|rabbits]], hares are generally larger, and their young are born fully furred with eyes open, able to fend for themselves soon after birth. All hares have 48 [[Chromosome|chromosomes]]. No hare has been domesticated. A hare less than one year old is called a leveret.

Sector of [[Orthodox Judaism]] characterized by a strict interpretation of religious sources and of [[Halakha|halakha]] (Jewish law). Haredim regard themselves as the most authentic custodians of Jewish law, which they consider binding and unchangeable. Many regard other contemporary expressions of Judaism, including Modern Orthodoxy, as deviations from God's laws, a view other movements dispute. The Hebrew term *haredi*, meaning "one who trembles" before God, is used in place of "ultra-Orthodox", a term many adherents consider pejorative. As of 2020 there were about 2.1 million Haredim worldwide, representing 14% of the world's Jewish population.

American exhibition [[Basketball|basketball]] team that combines athleticism, theater and [[Comedy|comedy]]. Originating in 1926 on the South Side of [[Chicago]], the team has played more than 26,000 exhibition games in 124 countries and territories, mostly against deliberately ineffective opponents such as the Washington Generals. Its signature song is Brother Bones' whistled version of "Sweet Georgia Brown", and its [[Mascot|mascot]] is an anthropomorphized globe named Globie. The team's first road trip, a 48-mile journey from Chicago to Hinckley, Illinois, was made in an uncomfortable [[Ford Model T]].

Area of [[Mathematical analysis|mathematical analysis]] concerned with decomposing functions into components based on symmetries, scales, spectra or oscillation. It grew out of the study of harmonic functions and their boundary behavior, and its basic examples are [[Fourier series]] and the [[Fourier transform]]. Modern harmonic analysis also studies maximal functions, singular integrals and spectral decompositions, and it has applications in signal processing. It differs from [[Fourier analysis]] chiefly in the functions considered and the questions addressed, since orthogonality alone is often not enough. The related tradition of abstract harmonic analysis studies functions and representations on topological groups, including Pontryagin duality. The field overlaps with [[Number theory]] and [[Functional analysis]].

Physical system in which a restoring force is proportional to displacement from equilibrium. Harmonic oscillators occur widely in nature, and any mass subject to a force in stable equilibrium acts as one for small vibrations. They are exploited in devices such as [[Clock|clocks]]. If the restoring force is the only force acting, the system undergoes simple harmonic motion, with sinusoidal oscillations of constant amplitude and a frequency independent of amplitude. Friction, or damping, can make the motion underdamped, critically damped or overdamped. In quantum mechanics, the [[Quantum harmonic oscillator|quantum harmonic oscillator]] has discrete energy levels, and its [[Potential energy|potential energy]] at displacement x is U = ½kx².

Free-reed [[Wind instrument|wind instrument]], also known as a French harp or mouth organ. Played worldwide in genres including [[Blues|blues]], [[Folk music|folk music]], [[Classical music|classical music]] and [[Jazz|jazz]], it makes sound when air blown into or drawn through its holes sets brass or steel reeds vibrating. The most common type is the diatonic, Richter-tuned instrument with ten air passages and twenty reeds, often called a blues harp. Players bend notes by adjusting their embouchure to lower the pitch of a reed. Combs were traditionally made of wood but are now also made of plastic or metal, including [[Titanium]] for high-end instruments. The instrument has also been popular in rock, with players such as [[Bob Dylan]].

Aspect of [[Music|music]] concerned with combining different sounds to create new musical ideas. Theories of harmony describe the effects of distinct pitches sounding together and identify chords, textures and tonalities. Harmony has a vertical dimension, the simultaneous sounds, and a horizontal dimension, the progression over time, and it overlaps with [[Melody|melody]], timbre and form. Harmony is central to Western music theory, in which a dissonant [[Chord (music)|chord]] typically resolves to a consonant one. Consonance has often been associated with simple mathematical ratios between pitch frequencies. The term derives from the Greek *harmonia*, meaning "joint, agreement, concord". [[Counterpoint]], which describes the relationship between independent melodic lines, is sometimes distinguished from harmony.

Prime Minister of the United Kingdom and [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative]] Party leader, 1957–1963. Nicknamed "Supermac", he succeeded [[Anthony Eden]] after the [[Suez Crisis]] and led the Conservatives to a larger majority in 1959. He presided over much of the [[Decolonization|decolonization]] of Africa, beginning with [[Ghana]] in 1957, and cited the "wind of change blowing across the continent". His government was rocked by the Profumo affair, and he resigned in October 1963, citing ill health.

English doctor and [[Serial killer|serial killer]]. A general practitioner, Shipman was convicted in 2000 of murdering 15 patients in his care and was sentenced to [[Life imprisonment|life imprisonment]] with a whole life order. He is considered one of the most prolific serial killers in modern history. The Shipman Inquiry, chaired by Dame Janet Smith, revealed that he targeted vulnerable elderly patients, killing them with fatal doses of drugs or by prescribing abnormal amounts. He took his own life in prison in [[West Yorkshire]].

American physical chemist, awarded the 1934 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for discovering heavy hydrogen. He studied thermodynamics under [[Gilbert N. Lewis]] at the University of California, Berkeley. His work on isotope separation led to the discovery of deuterium in 1931. During World War II he headed the group at [[Columbia University]] that developed gaseous diffusion for uranium enrichment, which became the sole method used in the early postwar period. At the [[University of Chicago]], his graduate student Stanley L. Miller showed that sparks passed through a mixture of [[Ammonia|ammonia]], [[Methane|methane]] and hydrogen, with water, produce [[Amino acid|amino acids]]. Urey later examined lunar samples from [[Apollo 11]].

Prime Minister of the [[United Kingdom]] (1964–1970; 1974–1976) and leader of the [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour Party]]. He is the only Labour leader to have formed a government after a general election four separate times. His government devalued the pound in 1967, liberalized [[Birth control|birth control]] and abortion law, abolished capital punishment and nationalized the steel sector. He refused to commit British troops to the [[Vietnam War]], but sent them to [[Northern Ireland]] in 1969, a move that contributed to escalating [[The Troubles|the Troubles]]. He resigned in 1976 citing worsening mental and physical health and later suffered from [[Alzheimer's disease]].

Stringed instrument whose strings run at an angle to its soundboard and are plucked with the fingers. Harps are usually wooden and triangular, and some have multiple rows of strings and pedals. The earliest harps and lyres were found in [[Sumer]], c. 2500 BCE, with harps excavated from royal tombs in [[Ur]]. Angular harps appeared in the [[Iraq]]–[[Iran]] region around 1900 BCE, and harps later spread across Europe and the Americas, where they remain part of [[Folk music|folk music]]. Historically, strings were made of sinew from [[Tendon|tendons]], gut, plant fiber or silk, and later of nylon and wire. The modern double-action pedal harp, developed in the early 19th century by Sébastien Érard, has 47 strings.

[[Keyboard instrument]] whose strings are plucked rather than struck. Pressing a key raises a jack holding a small plectrum, usually of quill or plastic, which plucks a string. Because the sound is fixed, a note sounds equally loud however hard the key is pressed. The harpsichord was widely used in Renaissance and [[Baroque music|Baroque]] music, both as a solo instrument and as part of the continuo. Italian makers evolved a design that survived into later centuries, and the Ruckers family of the Southern Netherlands built the first harpsichords with two keyboards. Around 1700 Bartolomeo Cristofori built the first [[Piano|piano]], and by the late 18th century the piano had largely supplanted the harpsichord. Revived in the 20th century, it is used in historically informed performances of music by [[Johann Sebastian Bach|Bach]] and others.

Large neotropical species of [[Eagle|eagle]], *Harpia harpyja*. It is the largest [[Bird of prey|bird of prey]] throughout its range and usually inhabits tropical lowland [[Rainforest|rainforest]], nesting and hunting in the emergent canopy. It is found from southern Mexico to as far south as Argentina, and preys on [[Sloth|sloths]], [[Opossum|opossums]] and other arboreal mammals. Destruction of its habitat has caused it to vanish from many parts of its former range, and it is nearly extirpated from much of Central America. [[Carl Linnaeus]] first described it in the 1758 *Systema Naturae*, and its name comes from the harpies of [[Greek mythology]].

American abolitionist and social activist. Born into slavery in Dorchester County, Maryland, Tubman escaped to [[Philadelphia]] in 1849 and returned repeatedly to rescue relatives and others. Known as "Moses", she made some 13 missions on the Underground Railroad to rescue approximately 70 enslaved people, and later said she "never lost a passenger". She met [[John Brown (abolitionist)|John Brown]] in 1858 and helped plan his 1859 raid on Harpers Ferry. During the [[American Civil War]] she served the Union Army as a nurse, cook, armed scout and spy. She is widely credited as the first woman to lead an armed military operation in the United States, the Combahee Ferry raid, which liberated more than 700 enslaved people. In later years she campaigned for [[Women's suffrage|women's suffrage]].
